questions.problem:
Consider the functions $y:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,f(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]?$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
$42$ {{field-4}} $18$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}+{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ {y}_{2} & {y}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}1\cdot 2\cdot 3 \\ 1+2+3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 & 3 \\ 42 & 24 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the functions $y:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,f(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}]. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
$4$ {{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{1} \\ 2{y}_{1} & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}({0}^{2}+{2}^{2}) \\ 0+2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(\frac{1}{2}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(\frac{1}{2}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 4 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{2}-{y}_{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 1 \\ -1 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2(-1) & 1 \\ -1 & 2(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
